respStmt.name: Angelo Mai and Carlo Ottavio Castiglioni

publicationStmt.authority: The textual legacy of the Ostrogoths in Italy: The Bible version and other texts (Acronym: LegOst)

availability.p: Not to ricirculate. Contact the LegOst Project researchers for more information.

summary.p: Gothic palimpsest preserving part of the Book of Nehemiah (5:13-18; 6:14-7:3; 7:13-45). This is the only manuscript that transmits part of the Old Testament in direct tradition. The upper Latin text transmits the Libri Regum.

extent.p: The fragment consists of the third bifolium from the outside and the last leaf of the same quire. The margins have been irregularly trimmed. The written area, consisting of 19 lines, measures approximately 108 × 156-158 mm.

foliation.p: The leaves are not numbered. Modern foliation is by page.

condition.p: The bifolium is now disbound and kept in a folder. Overlap with other leaves has caused phenomena of ink transfer onto the surviving leaves. Some portions are partially or completely illegible, often as a result of the use of chemical reagents, which have corroded the ink and caused holes in the parchment. The margins are severely damaged, possibly due to rodent activity, and a hole is present on p. 452.

layout.p: The Gothic text is written in a single column, in scriptio continua. The ruling was executed dry-point, with the aid of pricking marks, apparently on the unfolded bifolium. The written area is delimited by a single vertical ruling line.

handDesc.handNote: The Gothic text is written in the slanted Gothic script (with <s> of Greek or runic form) by a single scribe. The inclination of the letter axis, however, is only faintly marked. The stroke is heavy, and the usual rounding at the baseline is lacking. Letters of larger module occur, shifted to the left and entirely outside the vertical ruling, marking the beginning of a new textual unit.
The upper Latin text was written in different scripts: uncial, semi-uncial, and Insular majuscule (CLA, III 344b).

scriptDesc.p: The Gothic script is slanted Gothic with <s> of Greek or runic form. Letters of larger module mark the beginning of textual units, projecting beyond the ruling. Dark ink used (not more precisely identifiable).

additions.p: No quire number indicating the order of the gathering is visible on the last leaf of the quire.
Punctuation: The medial point marks minor pauses (commata), and the colon marks major pauses (cola).

Abbreviations: Both nasals are abbreviated at line end: <n> by means of a short horizontal stroke thickened at both ends, while the abbreviation mark for <m> is now almost completely illegible. Prior to the production of multispectral images (2025), the abbreviation for <m> had never been noticed. In addition, also at line end, the ligature <m>-<a> occurs (f. 451, l. 2). Nomina sacra are present.

Numerals: Numerous numerals are attested. In most cases, individual numerals—indicating hundreds, tens, and units—are placed between points. The supralinear stroke, generally used to mark numerals, is completely faded in most cases.
Corrections: Several corrections are visible, in the form of letters added in the interlinear space. Not all errors were corrected.
Orthography: No differences from the orthography of other Gothic manuscripts are attested.

origin.origDate: First third/first half of the sixth century (Gothic undertext)
Second half of the seventh century (Latin overtext)
origin.origPlace: It is highly likely that the original manuscript was copied in an Ostrogothic milieu. It was undoubtedly overwritten at Bobbio (CLA, III 344b; Zironi 2004, 63).

provenance.p: This is the only manuscript that transmits part of the Old Testament in direct tradition. The identification of the text has posed difficulties, as it preserves a list of populations returning from the Babylonian exile, transmitted in very similar form in both Ezra and Nehemiah. Apart from some dissenting opinions (Landau 2011), the identification of the text as Nehemiah now appears to be established (Snædal-Petersen 2012, 2017; Sigismund 2013; Heinzle 2016). The Gothic leaves, together with leaves containing two works by Seneca (Medea, Oedipus), were reused in the second half of the seventh century at Bobbio to restore a palimpsest of the second half of the sixth century which transmitted Plautus' Fabulae (Zironi 2004, 58-59, 63). This manuscript does not appear in the Bobbio catalogue of 1461.

acquisition.p: The undertext was discovered by Angelo Mai around 1815, but it was deciphered and identified as part of Ezra and Nehemiah only in 1817; on that occasion chemical reagents were used (Lo Monaco 1996, 689). It was published in 1819 together with Carlo Ottavio Castiglioni (Ulphilae partium ineditarum in Ambrosianis palimpsestis ab Angelo Maio repertarum specimen, jointly edited by Mai and Castiglioni, Milan, 2-7). The phototypic reproduction of the leaves was published by Jan de Vries in 1936.

surrogates.p: Phototypic reproduction in de Vries 1936. Multispectral images produced in 2025.

projectDesc.p: Progetto PRIN 2022 PNRR - Missione 4 "Istruzione e Ricerca" del Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza; missione 4, componente 1 – investimento 1.1, Fondo per il Programma Nazionale di Ricerca e Progetti di Rilevante Interesse Nazionale (PRIN), dal titolo The textual legacy of the Ostrogoths in Italy: The Bible version and other texts (Acronym: LegOst) - CUP J53D23013530006 - finanziato dall'Unione Europea-Next Generation EU.

Il progetto si compone di due unità di ricerca e di un consulente esterno:
Unità di Perugia: prof.ssa Carla Falluomini (PI), dott. Pierandrea Gottardi, dott. John Gallagher
Unità di Cagliari: prof. Antonio Piras, dott. Giacomo Bucci
consulente esterno: prof. Roberto Rosselli Del Turco (Università di Torino)
